thread.title: Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway Keeps Hitting New Highs—and It Still Looks Underpriced

author: Andrew Bary
title: Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway Keeps Hitting New Highs—and It Still Looks Underpriced
text:
Photo: Daniel Acker/Bloomberg By Andrew Bary Updated Sept. 21, 2018 11:05 p.m. ET Warren Buffett’s conglomerate has ended the summer as a red-hot stock.
Class A shares of Berkshire Hathaway (ticker: BRK.A) have risen 15% since July 17, when the company announced that it would relax restrictions on its stock buyback program. Last week, the shares touched three consecutive record highs, before closing on Friday at $331,336. The B shares finished at $220.52.
While there hasn’t been any major news to account for the recent advance in Berkshire shares, it’s clear that investors like the more flexible policy on stock buybacks.
A decade after the financial crisis, billionaire investor Warren Buffett explains what was behind the 2008 mayhem, what we can do to limit the damage and opportunities missed last time. The new guidelines allow Berkshire to repurchase stock when Buffett and Charlie Munger, the vice chairman, believe that the shares are trading below their view of intrinsic value, “conservatively determined.”
Berkshire has bought “a little” stock under the new authorization, Buffett told CNBC on Aug. 30—his 88th birthday— but he didn’t provide any more specifics.
Barron’s argued in a cover story in June (“Preparing Berkshire for a Future Without Buffett”) that Berkshire should lift its cap on share repurchases as a way to return more cash to shareholders. The company is sitting on more than $100 billion in cash.
Hopes for buybacks are just part of the Berkshire story. The Class A shares are now up 11% this year, topping the S&P 500, which has gained almost 10%.
David Rolfe, the chief investment officer of Wedgewood Partners in St. Louis, says that Berkshire investors “are putting the pieces of the puzzle together” and coming up with a higher valuation on the shares at a time when many value-oriented stocks are starting to rally. (Berkshire is one of Wedgewood’s largest holdings.)
He values the B shares at about $275, which would put the A shares above $400,000. Rolfe notes the strengths of rivals that mirror Berkshire units.
In particular, he points to Union Pacific (UNP), whose shares are up about 10% this month. Berkshire’s Burlington Northern railroad unit and Union Pacific dominate the market west of the Mississippi River. Another winner this year has been auto insurer Progressive (PGR), a prime competitor of Berkshire’s Geico unit. Progressive is up 25% this year. Geico’s revenues are about 10% above Progressive’s. The two are viewed as the best-managed auto insurers in the country, and both have been growing quickly.
Because its mix of businesses is focused on the U.S., Berkshire is benefiting broadly from the strength of the economy. This was evident in Berkshire’s strong second-quarter operating earnings, which were up 67%, to $6.9 billion.
With its slew of domestic-oriented units, Berkshire has also been a big winner from the lower corporate tax rate.
Newsletter Sign-up The company’s equity portfolio, which totaled about $192 billion at the end of the second quarter, has some winners, as well, with Apple (AAPL) topping the $1 trillion market-value threshold recently.
Berkshire held 258 million shares of Apple at the end of the second quarter, a stake now worth $57 billion, making it by far its largest equity holding. Buffett told CNBC last month that Berkshire had added slightly to the Apple holding since June 30.
American Express (AXP), another sizable Berkshire holding, has hit new 52-week highs lately, but Kraft Heinz (KHC) and Wells Fargo (WFC), other big Berkshire investments, have declined this year and badly lagged behind many of their peers.
“Berkshire is not a screaming bargain,” says Wedgewood’s Rolfe, “but it’s still undervalued.”
